title: Coral Reef Presumed Dead for 60 Years Rediscovered Alive and Thriving Off the Coast of Benin
excerpt: Underwater drones deployed by Beninese scientists found a deep-water coral ecosystem teeming with life in the Gulf of Guinea, more than six decades after surveys dismissed it as a dead formation.
body:
• A coral reef off the coast of Benin, presumed dead since the 1960s, has been rediscovered alive using modern sonar and underwater drone technology.
  • The mesophotic coral ecosystem, sitting more than 50 meters below the surface, hosts at least eight coral types and eight fish species.
  • The discovery, published in Frontiers in Marine Science, is the first confirmed record of a living mesophotic coral ecosystem on the Gulf of Guinea continental shelf.
  • Researchers believe the reef may be part of a larger system stretching nearly 25 miles parallel to the Benin coastline.

A deep-ocean coral reef that scientists had written off as dead more than 60 years ago has been rediscovered alive and thriving off the coast of Benin in West Africa, in a finding that underscores how much remains unknown about the world's underwater ecosystems.

A team of oceanographers led by Gérard Zinzindohoué at the Institut de Recherches Halieutiques et Océanologiques du Bénin documented their findings in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science, revealing a healthy deep-water coral community more than 50 meters (164 feet) below the surface of the Gulf of Guinea.

"I still remember seeing those first images. It was a mix of excitement and disbelief, because after all this time thinking about this reef, suddenly there was something real in front of us."

— Gérard Zinzindohoué, Institut de Recherches Halieutiques et Océanologiques du Bénin

A Reef Lost to Science

Scientists first identified the possible reef location during the 1960s while surveying potential fishing areas in the Gulf of Guinea. Limited by the technology of the era, they concluded that whatever coral formation existed along the seafloor was dead. The reef then vanished from the scientific record for more than half a century.

The rediscovery came after Zinzindohoué and his colleagues received grant funding to revisit the area. The team spent days scanning 11.5 kilometers (7.1 miles) of seabed using side-scan sonar before flagging two signals large enough to match potential reef remnants.

"It was not an easy field campaign," Zinzindohoué recalled. "It was a mix of long days at sea, technical problems, and a lot of uncertainty. But then we saw structures on the sonar that looked like they could be reef signatures, which gave us hope that we were close."

Alive Against the Odds

The team then deployed an underwater drone and the National Geographic Exploration Technology Lab's Deep Sea Camera System. About 50 meters below the ocean surface, they found what decades of assumption had denied: the reef was far from dead.

The ecosystem is classified as a mesophotic coral community — a type of reef found at the limit of where sunlight can penetrate, in the transition zone between shallower waters and the deep ocean. These systems are historically understudied compared to their shallow-water counterparts.

Footage revealed at least eight distinct coral types, dominated by octocorals forming a coral garden. Eight fish species were documented using the habitat, including golden African snappers, blackbar soldierfish, Guinean angelfish, West African goatfish, the Monrovia doctorfish, three-banded butterflyfish, and two damselfish species.

Potentially Much Larger

The examined region may be part of a much larger system stretching nearly 25 miles (40 kilometers) parallel to the Benin coastline, according to the researchers. The discovery is the first confirmed record of a living mesophotic coral ecosystem on the Gulf of Guinea continental shelf.

"I think what we found is probably not an exception," Zinzindohoué said. "It is more likely a reflection of how little we still know about coastal regions in West Africa and elsewhere. If we were able to find this reef again after 60 years, how many others are still undocumented or simply forgotten?"

A Rare Bright Spot for Coral Science

The finding arrives at a time when coral reefs worldwide face mounting threats from climate change, ocean acidification, and pollution. While shallow-water reefs have dominated conservation conversations, mesophotic ecosystems may serve as refuges for marine biodiversity as surface waters warm.

For scientists and conservationists across the global south, including India — which has its own understudied mesophotic reef systems along the Lakshadweep and Andaman coasts — the Benin discovery is a reminder that exploration, not just protection, remains an urgent priority in marine science.
